name: VitaCore FlowGuard Hemodynamic Regulator
body_location: subdermal thoracic — mounted adjacent to the aortic arch via minimally invasive thoracoscopic insertion
description:
The VitaCore FlowGuard is a subdermal hemodynamic management implant designed to continuously monitor and regulate arterial blood pressure in real time. A mesh of piezoelectric microsensors threads along the outer aortic wall and carotid branches, feeding data to a central microprocessor roughly the size of a flattened grape. When pressure deviates beyond calibrated thresholds — upward during stress events, downward during orthostatic drops — the FlowGuard releases nanodose vasodilators or vasoconstrictors from an integrated reservoir capsule, replenished via quarterly subcutaneous injection at any VitaCore-licensed pharmacy. The system also logs rolling 90-day cardiovascular data to the user's health profile, flagging anomalies for review by a licensed practitioner or the user's personal med-AI.

The FlowGuard is, in the parlance of GLMZ's working-class neighborhoods, simply 'the thing that keeps you from dropping.' Hypertension runs deep in Tier 1 and 2 populations — stress, poor food access, environmental pollutants, shift work that never ends — and the FlowGuard has become as commonplace as corrective lenses once were. Tier 2 factory workers get them subsidized through employer wellness mandates. Older residents on the Shelf scrape together installment payments through VitaCore's LifeCredit program. The implant doesn't cure the conditions that drive high blood pressure; it simply keeps the body from catastrophizing while life continues at its brutal pace. For many users, the most notable daily experience is an absence: no more afternoon headaches behind the eyes, no more waking dizzy, no more sitting down on the transit platform because the world went gray.
installation_requirements: Outpatient surgical clinic; thoracoscopic procedure under local anesthesia, approximately 90 minutes; requires a licensed VitaCore implant technician or cardiovascular nurse practitioner
maintenance: Quarterly reservoir refill injection at any licensed VitaCore pharmacy kiosk (self-administered or assisted); annual firmware sync and sensor calibration at clinic; reservoir capsule replacement every 3 years

side_effects: Mild lightheadedness during the first two weeks as the system calibrates to baseline pressure
Occasional sensation of warmth in the chest following a vasodilator release event
Vivid or unusually detailed dreams reported during initial calibration period
Rare: minor bruising at the thoracic insertion site that persists up to three weeks post-installation
cultural_context: In GLMZ, the FlowGuard occupies the same social register as reading glasses or a knee brace — medical, necessary, and almost invisible. On the Shelf and in Tier 2 districts, it carries a slight connotation of hard living: if you have one, people assume your body has been ground down by work or stress or bad luck, and there is no shame in that assumption because it is usually true. In Tier 3 and above, the FlowGuard is sometimes replaced by more expensive whole-system cardiovascular suites from Helix or Lazarus, and wearing a VitaCore implant in those circles can read as a subtle class marker — functional, reliable, but unmistakably budget-line. Street-level pharmacies in Tier 1 often display the FlowGuard refill injectors in open cases near the counter, the way aspirin once sat on drugstore shelves, normalized to the point of invisibility.
known_users: Tier 1 and 2 adults over 35 managing chronic hypertension
Shift workers in industrial and logistics sectors
Elderly residents on fixed-income VitaCore LifeCredit plans
Middle-aged Tier 3 professionals managing stress-related cardiovascular risk
People with family histories of stroke or cardiac events who want passive protection
story_hooks: A character's FlowGuard begins releasing vasodilators at random during moments of calm — someone has remotely tampered with the firmware, and whoever it is seems to know exactly when the character is meeting with someone important.

A Tier 1 pharmacy kiosk is offering FlowGuard refill injectors at half price, sourced from an unlicensed supplier. People are taking them. Two users have already been hospitalized with pressure crashes. The source needs to be found before more people get hurt.

A VitaCore LifeCredit collections agent is repossessing FlowGuard implants from delinquent accounts — a process that requires a brief surgical extraction. A community health worker needs help stopping the removals, or at least documenting them.
